source: Adapted revision checklist based on VCAA's VCE Applied Computing Study Design, Units 3 and 4 Data Analytics. Checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs, not VCAA syllabus numbering. Legislation changes, so verify legal detail against current sources.

points.area: The problem-solving methodology
points.title: The four stages
points.detail: Analysis, design, development and evaluation, the activities within each stage, and the iterative rather than strictly linear nature of the process.

questions.q: Name the four stages of the problem-solving methodology and the activities within each.
answer: Analysis: solution requirements, constraints and scope.
Design: solution design and evaluation criteria.
Development: manipulation, validation, testing and documentation.
Evaluation: the strategy for evaluating the solution, and the evaluation itself against the criteria established during design.

points.area: The problem-solving methodology
points.title: Solution requirements, constraints and scope
points.detail: Distinguishing functional from non-functional requirements, identifying economic, technical, social, legal and usability constraints, and defining boundaries.

questions.q: Distinguish between functional and non-functional requirements and give an example of each for a data visualisation solution.
answer: Functional requirements describe what the solution must do, such as filtering sales data by region and generating a comparative chart.
Non-functional requirements describe how well it must do it, covering qualities such as usability, response time, accessibility and reliability.
A functional example is that the solution must allow the user to select a date range.
A non-functional example is that the visualisation must be readable by a viewer with colour vision deficiency.

points.area: The problem-solving methodology
points.title: Evaluation criteria
points.detail: Writing measurable criteria derived from the solution requirements, covering effectiveness and efficiency, before development begins.

questions.q: Explain why evaluation criteria are written during the design stage rather than after development, and what makes a criterion measurable.
answer: Criteria written during design are derived from the solution requirements rather than from what the solution happens to do.
Writing them afterwards risks describing the finished product rather than testing whether it met the need.
A measurable criterion states a specific, testable standard, such as whether a user can locate a given figure within 30 seconds.
Vague criteria such as 'the solution looks good' cannot be tested and produce no useful evaluation.

points.area: The problem-solving methodology
points.title: Effectiveness and efficiency
points.detail: The measures of effectiveness including completeness, accuracy, readability, clarity, attractiveness, timeliness, communication of message, relevance and usability, and the measures of efficiency including time, cost and effort.

questions.q: Distinguish between effectiveness and efficiency and name three measures of each.
answer: Effectiveness measures how well the solution meets the user's needs and achieves its purpose.
Measures of effectiveness include accuracy, completeness, readability, clarity, attractiveness, timeliness, communication of message, relevance and usability.
Efficiency measures the resources consumed in producing or using the solution.
Measures of efficiency include the time taken, the cost incurred and the effort or labour required.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Data and information
points.detail: Data as raw unprocessed facts and information as data that has been processed and given meaning in a context.

questions.q: Distinguish between data and information, using an example from a sales dataset.
answer: Data consists of raw, unorganised facts with no context, such as the individual figures 4200, 3900 and 5100.
Information is data that has been processed, organised and placed in a context so it has meaning.
Stating that quarterly sales rose from 3900 to 5100 dollars in the Melbourne store, an increase of 31 per cent, converts the data into information usable for a decision.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Types and characteristics of data
points.detail: Numeric, text, Boolean, date and time, image, audio and video data types, and structured, semi-structured and unstructured data.

questions.q: Explain the difference between structured and unstructured data and give an example of each.
answer: Structured data is organised into a predefined format such as rows and columns or defined fields, which makes it directly searchable and analysable.
A relational database table of customer transactions is structured data.
Unstructured data has no predefined model, such as free-text survey responses, emails, images or video, and must be processed before it can be analysed.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Primary and secondary data sources
points.detail: Collecting data directly through surveys, interviews, observation and sensors, or obtaining it from existing datasets, and the advantages of each.

questions.q: Compare primary and secondary data collection, giving one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
answer: Primary data is collected first-hand for the specific purpose, so it matches the requirements exactly and its collection method is known.
Its disadvantage is that collection is time consuming and expensive, and the sample may be small.
Secondary data already exists, so it is faster and cheaper to obtain and often covers a much larger population.
Its disadvantage is that it was collected for another purpose, so its currency, scope and reliability must be assessed before use.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Collection methods and sampling
points.detail: Designing surveys and forms, using sensors and logs, and selecting a sample that represents the population being investigated.

questions.q: Explain three features of a well-designed online survey used to collect primary data.
answer: Questions are unambiguous and neutral, avoiding leading wording that biases responses.
Closed questions with defined options produce structured data that can be analysed directly, while open questions capture detail but require processing.
Input constraints such as drop-down lists, radio buttons and required fields improve data integrity at the point of entry.
The sample must be large enough and selected so it represents the population the conclusions will describe.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Data integrity
points.detail: Accuracy, authenticity, correctness, reasonableness, relevance and timeliness as characteristics of data with integrity, and the consequences of poor integrity.

questions.q: Name four characteristics of data integrity and explain the consequence of using data that lacks timeliness.
answer: Characteristics include accuracy, authenticity, correctness, reasonableness, relevance and timeliness.
Accuracy means the data correctly reflects what it claims to measure; authenticity means its source is genuine and verifiable.
Timeliness means the data is current enough for the decision being made.
Out-of-date data produces conclusions about conditions that no longer apply, so a decision based on it may be wrong even though the analysis was performed correctly.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Validation techniques
points.detail: Existence, type and range checks, and the distinction between manual and electronic validation.

questions.q: Name the three validation techniques and give an example of each applied to a date of birth field.
answer: Existence check: confirms the field is not left blank, so a record cannot be saved without a date of birth.
Type check: confirms the entry is a valid date rather than text or a number.
Range check: confirms the date falls within acceptable limits, such as not being in the future and not implying an age over 120.
Validation reduces errors at entry but cannot detect a value that is valid yet incorrect, which requires verification against a source.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Cleaning and preparing data
points.detail: Removing duplicates, handling missing values, correcting inconsistent formats and outliers, and documenting every change made.

questions.q: Describe three data cleaning tasks and explain why cleaning must be documented.
answer: Removing duplicate records so that entries are not counted more than once in aggregations.
Standardising inconsistent formats, such as dates entered in different orders or state names entered in several forms.
Deciding how to handle missing values, either by exclusion or by a documented substitution rule.
Documentation is required so the analysis can be reproduced and so that decisions affecting the results, such as excluding outliers, are transparent and justifiable.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Manipulating and analysing data
points.detail: Sorting, filtering, aggregating, calculating derived fields, cross-tabulating and identifying patterns, relationships and anomalies.

questions.q: Explain the difference between sorting, filtering and aggregating, and give a purpose for each.
answer: Sorting orders records by the values in one or more fields, which helps identify highest and lowest values and reveals ranking.
Filtering displays only records meeting specified conditions, which isolates a subset such as a single region or date range.
Aggregating combines records into summary values such as totals, means or counts by group.
Aggregation converts many rows of raw data into the summary figures a visualisation can communicate.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Data, information and analysis
points.title: Patterns, relationships and interpretation
points.detail: Identifying trends, correlations, clusters and outliers in data, and distinguishing a genuine relationship from a coincidental one.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a correlation and a causal relationship, and why the distinction matters for a data analyst.
answer: A correlation means two variables change together in a consistent pattern.
A causal relationship means a change in one variable directly produces a change in the other.
A correlation may arise from coincidence or from a third variable that influences both.
Presenting a correlation as causation in a visualisation misleads the audience into a decision the data does not support, which is both an accuracy and an ethical failure.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Designing data visualisations
points.title: Purpose and audience
points.detail: Identifying what the visualisation must communicate and to whom, and letting that determine the level of detail, terminology and presentation.

questions.q: Explain how the intended audience affects the design of a data visualisation.
answer: A specialist audience can interpret dense charts and technical terminology, so more detail can be presented at once.
A general audience needs a single clear message per chart, plain labelling and explanatory annotation.
Audience also determines the medium and format, such as a printed infographic for the public against an interactive dashboard for analysts.
Designing without a defined audience usually produces a visualisation that displays data rather than communicating a message.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Designing data visualisations
points.title: Selecting the right chart type
points.detail: Matching the chart to the relationship being shown: comparison, composition, distribution, relationship or change over time.

questions.q: State the appropriate chart type for showing change over time, comparison between categories and the relationship between two numeric variables, and justify one choice.
answer: Change over time is best shown with a line chart, since the connected line implies continuity between points.
Comparison between categories is best shown with a bar or column chart, where length is easy to compare accurately.
The relationship between two numeric variables is best shown with a scatter plot.
A line chart is inappropriate for unordered categories because connecting them implies a progression that does not exist.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Designing data visualisations
points.title: Design elements
points.detail: The use of point, line, shape, texture, size, colour and value in creating a visualisation.

questions.q: Explain how colour and size can be used as design elements to direct attention in a visualisation.
answer: Colour creates contrast, so a single saturated colour against a muted palette draws the eye to the most important data series.
Size signals importance, so the most significant chart or figure should occupy the largest area.
Both must be used consistently, since a colour that means one thing in one chart and something else in another confuses the viewer.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Designing data visualisations
points.title: Design principles
points.detail: Alignment, repetition, contrast, space, balance and hierarchy, and their application to layout and readability.

questions.q: Explain the design principles of hierarchy and repetition and how each improves a data visualisation.
answer: Hierarchy orders elements by importance so the viewer knows what to read first, established through size, position, weight and colour.
Without hierarchy every element competes for attention and the main message is lost.
Repetition reuses consistent fonts, colours, spacing and chart styles across the visualisation.
This creates a unified appearance and reduces the effort required to interpret each new element.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Designing data visualisations
points.title: Design tools
points.detail: Annotated diagrams, mock-ups, storyboards, data dictionaries and input-process-output charts, and the purpose of each.

questions.q: Distinguish between a mock-up and a storyboard, and state what each communicates to a developer.
answer: A mock-up shows the appearance and layout of a single screen or page, including the position, size and formatting of each element.
A storyboard shows the structure of a multi-page solution and the navigation links between pages.
A mock-up communicates what each screen should look like; a storyboard communicates how the user moves between them.
Both are annotated so that formatting, data sources and interactive behaviour are specified rather than inferred.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Designing data visualisations
points.title: Data dictionaries
points.detail: Documenting each field's name, data type, size, format, description, validation rules and example values.

questions.q: State four items recorded in a data dictionary and explain its purpose.
answer: The field name, the data type, the field size and the format, such as a date pattern or number of decimal places.
A description of what the field stores, any validation rules that apply and an example value.
Its purpose is to specify the structure of the data so that a developer creates the solution consistently.
It also documents integrity requirements, so the same validation is applied wherever the data is entered or imported.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Designing data visualisations
points.title: Design for accessibility and readability
points.detail: Contrast ratios, colour-blind safe palettes, text size, alternative text and not relying on colour alone to convey meaning.

questions.q: Explain three design decisions that make a visualisation accessible to a viewer with colour vision deficiency.
answer: Do not rely on colour alone to distinguish data series; add direct labels, patterns or distinct line styles as a second cue.
Choose a colour-blind safe palette, avoiding red and green as the only distinction between adjacent categories.
Ensure sufficient contrast between text and background so labels remain readable.
Testing the visualisation in greyscale is a quick way to confirm the message survives without colour.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Designing data visualisations
points.title: Misleading visualisations
points.detail: Truncated axes, inconsistent scales, inappropriate chart types, cherry-picked ranges and three-dimensional distortion.

questions.q: Explain how a truncated vertical axis can mislead, and name two other techniques that distort a data story.
answer: Truncating the vertical axis so it does not begin at zero exaggerates the apparent difference between bar heights.
A change of a few per cent can be made to look like a doubling, misrepresenting the significance of the difference.
Selecting a narrow date range that excludes contradictory data cherry-picks the evidence to support a predetermined conclusion.
Three-dimensional effects distort the perceived area of segments, and inconsistent scales between charts make invalid comparisons look valid.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Developing and evaluating solutions
points.title: Development of the solution
points.detail: Manipulating the data, applying formatting and functionality, and using software tools appropriate to the design specification.

questions.q: Explain why development should follow the design specification rather than proceeding directly from the data.
answer: The design was derived from the solution requirements, so following it keeps the solution aligned with the user's needs.
Departing from the design during development often produces a solution that displays whatever was easiest rather than what was required.
If a design cannot be implemented, the design should be revised and the change documented, so the evaluation criteria remain valid.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Developing and evaluating solutions
points.title: Testing
points.detail: Preparing a test table with test data, expected results and actual results, and using normal, boundary and invalid data.

questions.q: Describe the structure of a test table and explain why boundary and invalid data must be included.
answer: A test table records what is being tested, the test data used, the expected result, the actual result and the corrective action taken.
Normal data confirms the solution works under ordinary conditions.
Boundary data tests the values at the edges of an acceptable range, where off-by-one errors most commonly occur.
Invalid data confirms that validation rejects incorrect input rather than accepting or corrupting it.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Developing and evaluating solutions
points.title: Formats and conventions
points.detail: Applying consistent titles, axis labels, units, legends, number formats, fonts and source citations to visualisations.

questions.q: List five formats and conventions that must be applied to a chart and explain why source citation matters.
answer: A descriptive title stating what the chart shows, labelled axes including units, and a legend where more than one series appears.
Consistent number formatting, such as a fixed number of decimal places and thousands separators, and consistent fonts and colours.
A citation of the data source, including the date the data was obtained.
Citation allows the viewer to verify the data and assess its currency and reliability, and acknowledges the original creator as required by copyright.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Developing and evaluating solutions
points.title: Evaluation strategy and evaluation
points.detail: Planning what evidence will be collected, from whom and when, then evaluating the solution against the criteria set during design.

questions.q: Explain the difference between an evaluation strategy and an evaluation, and what evidence a strong evaluation uses.
answer: An evaluation strategy is the plan, specifying what data will be collected to assess each criterion, from which users and at what time after implementation.
The evaluation is the judgement itself, made after the solution has been used.
A strong evaluation addresses each criterion separately and reaches a clear judgement on whether it was met.
Evidence includes user feedback, observation of users completing tasks, timing data and testing results, rather than the developer's own impression.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Data and information security
points.title: Threats to data and information
points.detail: Accidental, deliberate and event-based threats, and examples of each including human error, malware, hacking and natural disaster.

questions.q: Classify the following threats and give one further example of each category: an employee emailing a file to the wrong address; a ransomware attack; a flood in the server room.
answer: Emailing a file to the wrong address is an accidental threat caused by human error; another example is deleting a file unintentionally.
A ransomware attack is a deliberate threat; other examples include hacking, phishing, insider theft and denial of service attacks.
A flood in the server room is an event-based threat; other examples include fire, power failure and hardware failure.
Each category requires different controls, so classifying the threat guides the choice of control.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Data and information security
points.title: Physical and software controls
points.detail: Locks, biometrics, surveillance, backup and secure disposal as physical controls; passwords, encryption, firewalls, antivirus and access rights as software controls.

questions.q: Distinguish between physical and software controls and give two examples of each.
answer: Physical controls restrict physical access to equipment and media, or protect it from environmental damage.
Examples include locked server rooms, swipe card access, surveillance cameras, backup media stored offsite and secure destruction of old drives.
Software controls operate within the computer system to restrict access to and protect data.
Examples include passwords and multi-factor authentication, encryption, firewalls, antivirus software and user access rights.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Data and information security
points.title: Encryption
points.detail: The purpose of encryption, the distinction between data at rest and data in transit, and the limits of what encryption protects.

questions.q: Explain how encryption protects data and what it does not protect against.
answer: Encryption converts readable data into an unreadable form that can only be returned to plain text with the correct key.
Data at rest is encrypted in storage, so a stolen device or drive yields no usable information.
Data in transit is encrypted while being transmitted, so intercepted traffic cannot be read.
Encryption does not protect against a legitimate user misusing their access, and it is ineffective if the key is weak, shared or stored alongside the data.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Data and information security
points.title: Authentication and access rights
points.detail: Passwords, multi-factor authentication and biometrics, and the principle of granting the minimum access each user requires.

questions.q: Explain the principle of least privilege and why multi-factor authentication is stronger than a password alone.
answer: The principle of least privilege grants each user only the access rights required to perform their role, and no more.
This limits the damage from a compromised account or a malicious insider, since the account cannot reach data outside its role.
Multi-factor authentication requires two or more of something you know, something you have and something you are.
A stolen password alone is therefore insufficient to gain access, which defeats most phishing and credential-theft attacks.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Data and information security
points.title: Backup, redundancy and disaster recovery
points.detail: Full, incremental and differential backups, the value of offsite and offline copies, and the components of a disaster recovery plan.

questions.q: Explain the difference between full and incremental backups and why an offsite copy matters.
answer: A full backup copies all selected data each time, which is slower and uses more storage but restores in a single step.
An incremental backup copies only the data changed since the last backup, which is faster but requires the full backup and every subsequent increment to restore.
An offsite copy protects against an event-based threat that destroys the premises, such as fire or flood.
An offline copy also protects against ransomware, which can encrypt connected backups along with the live data.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Data and information security
points.title: Risk management plans
points.detail: Identifying risks, assessing likelihood and consequence, and selecting controls to avoid, reduce, transfer or accept each risk.

questions.q: Describe the components of a risk management plan and explain how likelihood and consequence determine the response.
answer: Identify the risks to data and information, then assess each for likelihood of occurring and the consequence if it does.
Combine the two into a risk rating, so that resources are directed to the risks that matter most.
High likelihood and high consequence risks require immediate controls to reduce or avoid them.
Low likelihood and low consequence risks may be accepted, and some risks can be transferred, for example through insurance.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Data and information security
points.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of security strategies
points.detail: Judging strategies against the threats identified, the cost and usability trade-offs, and the need for review as threats change.

questions.q: Explain why the strongest available security control is not always the best choice for an organisation.
answer: Security controls impose costs in money, time and staff training that must be proportionate to the value of the data protected.
Controls that are onerous to use encourage staff to work around them, for example by writing passwords down or sharing accounts.
A workaround can create a larger vulnerability than the one the control addressed.
The appropriate control balances the risk rating, the cost and the effect on usability, and must be reviewed as threats change.

points.area: Legal and ethical obligations
points.title: Privacy obligations
points.detail: The collection, use, storage and disclosure of personal information, the requirement for consent, and the individual's right to access and correct their data.

questions.q: Explain four obligations an organisation has when it collects personal information.
answer: Collect only the personal information reasonably necessary for the stated purpose, rather than gathering all available data.
Inform the individual why the information is being collected and how it will be used, and obtain consent.
Store the information securely and take reasonable steps to protect it from misuse, loss and unauthorised access.
Use or disclose it only for the purpose for which it was collected, and allow individuals to access and correct their own information.

points.area: Legal and ethical obligations
points.title: Health records and sensitive information
points.detail: The additional obligations attaching to health and other sensitive information, and the consequences of a breach.

questions.q: Explain why health information is subject to stricter obligations than other personal information.
answer: Health information is sensitive because disclosure can lead to discrimination in employment, insurance and social settings.
It is rarely possible to remedy the harm once the information has been disclosed, unlike a compromised password that can be changed.
Stricter obligations therefore apply to consent, access, retention periods and the security controls required.

points.area: Legal and ethical obligations
points.title: Copyright and intellectual property
points.detail: The ownership of data, images, code and visualisations, the requirement to attribute sources, and the terms attaching to open datasets.

questions.q: Explain the copyright obligations that apply when using a government dataset and an image found online in a visualisation.
answer: Copyright protects the original expression of the creator, so material cannot simply be reused because it is publicly accessible.
A government dataset is typically released under a licence, commonly one requiring attribution, and the licence terms must be checked and followed.
An image found online is presumed to be protected unless a licence expressly permits reuse, so permission or a suitably licensed alternative is required.
Attribution of the source must be included in the visualisation regardless, both to meet licence terms and to support verifiability.

points.area: Legal and ethical obligations
points.title: Ethical use of data
points.detail: The difference between what is legal and what is ethical, informed consent, de-identification and the responsible presentation of findings.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a legal and an ethical obligation, and give an example where a legal action may still be unethical.
answer: A legal obligation is a requirement imposed by legislation, breach of which carries a penalty.
An ethical obligation arises from what is right and fair, and may extend beyond what the law requires.
Combining several legally obtained datasets can re-identify individuals who believed their data was anonymous, which may be lawful but is unethical.
Presenting a chart with a truncated axis to exaggerate a trend is similarly lawful but misleads the audience, breaching the obligation to represent data honestly.

points.area: Project management and exam technique
points.title: Project plans and Gantt charts
points.detail: Identifying tasks, durations, sequence, dependencies, milestones and the critical path, and monitoring progress against the plan.

questions.q: Explain what a Gantt chart shows and define a dependency and the critical path.
answer: A Gantt chart shows each task as a horizontal bar positioned by start date with length proportional to duration, against a calendar timeline.
A dependency exists where one task cannot begin until another finishes, shown by linking arrows between bars.
The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent tasks, which determines the minimum time for the whole project.
A delay to any task on the critical path delays the entire project, whereas a task with slack can be delayed without that effect.

points.area: Project management and exam technique
points.title: Monitoring and adjusting a project
points.detail: Comparing actual progress with the plan, identifying tasks at risk, and reallocating time or resources to protect the deadline.

questions.q: Explain what a student should do when a task on the critical path is running late.
answer: Recognise that the delay will push back the project completion date unless action is taken.
Consider reallocating time from tasks with slack, reducing scope in a non-essential area, or working on later tasks concurrently where dependencies allow.
Update the project plan to reflect the change, so the revised critical path and deadline are clear.

points.area: Project management and exam technique
points.title: Answering with the correct terminology
points.detail: Using precise terms such as validation rather than verification, effectiveness rather than efficiency, and data rather than information.

questions.q: Distinguish between validation and verification, and between effectiveness and efficiency.
answer: Validation checks that data entered is reasonable and in the correct form, for example that a date is a real date within range.
Verification checks that the data entered matches the original source, for example by proofreading against the source document.
Effectiveness is how well the solution meets the user's needs; efficiency is the resources it consumes.
A solution can be effective but inefficient if it produces the right result but takes far too long to use.

points.area: Project management and exam technique
points.title: Applying theory to a case study
points.detail: Using specific details from the scenario, naming the organisation, the data involved and the threat or requirement described.

questions.q: Explain why a generic answer about security controls scores poorly on a case study question.
answer: Marks are awarded for selecting the control appropriate to the specific threat and organisation described in the scenario.
A list of every control shows no judgement about which is relevant, and does not demonstrate understanding.
A strong response names the control, explains the specific mechanism by which it addresses the threat in that scenario, and refers to details given in the case.
